issue.issue_text: Whether the right to a speedy trial is a fundamental right implicit in Article 21 of the Constitution.

law.fact_text: The right to a speedy trial is a fundamental right implicit in Article 21 of the Constitution.
relevant_text: The right to speedy trial is a fundamental right implicit in Art. 21 of the Constitution.

law.fact_text: The Court reaffirmed its previous holding on this issue from the case of Hussainara Khatoon & Ors. v. Home Secretary, State of Bihar.
relevant_text: We have already held in Hussainara Khatoon & Ors. v. Home Secretary, State of Bihar, [1979] 3 SCR 169 that the right to speedy trial is a fundamental right implicit in Art. 21 of the Constitution.

application.fact_text: The Court reasoned that if an accused person is not tried speedily and their case remains pending for an unreasonable length of time, their fundamental right is violated.
relevant_text: If an accnsed is not tried speedily and "his case remains pending before the Magistrate or the Sessions Court for an unreasonable length of time, it is clear that his fundamental right to _J speedy trial would be violated

application.fact_text: The Court noted exceptions, stating that a violation would not occur if the delay was caused by an interim order from a superior court or if the accused was responsible for the delay.
relevant_text: ...unless, of course, the trial is held up on account of some interim order passed by a superior court or the accused is responsible for the delay in the trial of the case.

application.fact_text: The Court established that the consequence for violating the right to a speedy trial is that the prosecution itself is liable to be quashed.
relevant_text: The consequence of violation of the fundamental right to speedy trial would be that the prosecution itself would be liable to be quashed on the ground that it is in breach of the fundamental right.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the right to a speedy trial is a fundamental right implicit in Article 21 of the Constitution. It reasoned that an unreasonable delay in trial violates this right, and the consequence of such a violation is the quashing of the prosecution, unless the delay is attributable to a superior court's order or the accused themselves.

issue.issue_text: Whether the violation of the fundamental right to a speedy trial can result in the quashing of the prosecution.

facts: The case addresses the issue of delays in the criminal justice system, particularly concerning accused individuals whose cases remain pending for an unreasonable length of time.
law: The Supreme Court identified the right to a speedy trial as a fundamental right implicit in Article 21 of the Constitution of India.
application: The Court reasoned that if an accused person is not tried speedily and their case remains pending for an unreasonable amount of time, their fundamental right under Article 21 is violated.
It clarified that this violation would not occur if the delay is caused by an interim order from a superior court or if the accused person is responsible for the delay.

The Court explicitly stated that the direct "consequence of violation of the fundamental right to speedy trial would be that the prosecution itself would be liable to be quashed on the ground that it is in breach of the fundamental right."
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the violation of the fundamental right to a speedy trial can result in the quashing of the prosecution. It held that if a trial is delayed for an unreasonable period, and the delay is not caused by the accused or a superior court's order, the prosecution is liable to be quashed as a remedy for the breach of this fundamental right.

issue.issue_text: Whether specific time limits should be set for the investigation and trial of offences committed by children.

facts: The Court observed that children accused of offences were being detained in jail for long periods.
These delays were caused by slow police investigations and protracted trials.
law: The Court relied on the fundamental right to a speedy trial, which it held is implicit in Article 21 of the Constitution.
application: The Court reasoned that to prevent children from being held in jail for long periods and to uphold their right to a speedy trial, specific time limits were necessary.
It found no reason why investigations and trials involving children could not be completed quickly.
The Court established a clear timeline for cases where a child is accused of an offence punishable with imprisonment of not more than 7 years.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the issue and set specific time limits. For offences committed by children (punishable with imprisonment of not more than 7 years), the investigation must be completed within a maximum of 3 months from the filing of the complaint or FIR. Following the filing of the charge sheet, the trial must be completed within a further 6 months. The Court ruled that if these deadlines are not met, the prosecution against the child would be liable to be quashed.

cases.case_name: Hussainara Khatoon & Ors. v. Home Secretary, State of Bihar
cases.principle: The right to speedy trial is a fundamental right implicit in Art. 21 of the Constitution.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The right to a speedy trial is a fundamental right implicit in Article 21 of the Constitution. If an accused is not tried speedily and their case remains pending for an unreasonable length of time, their fundamental right is violated, unless the delay is caused by an interim order from a superior court or by the accused's own actions. The consequence of such a violation is that the prosecution itself is liable to be quashed.
obiter: Every State Government must take necessary measures for the purpose of setting up an adequate number of courts, appointing the requisite number of Judges, and providing them with the necessary facilities.
It is also necessary to set up an Institute or Academy for the training of judicial officers.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court reaffirmed that the right to a speedy trial is a fundamental right implicit in Article 21 of the Constitution, the violation of which results in the quashing of the prosecution. To give this right practical effect for children, the court established specific and mandatory time limits for cases involving a child accused of an offence punishable with not more than 7 years imprisonment: three months for the investigation and six months for the trial from the filing of the chargesheet. If these deadlines are not met, the prosecution against the child must be quashed.
legal_tests_applied: The right to a speedy trial is a fundamental right implicit in Art. 21 of the Constitution. If an accused is not tried speedily and his case remains pending for an unreasonable length of time, his fundamental right is violated.
The consequence of violation of the fundamental right to speedy trial would be that the prosecution itself would be liable to be quashed on the ground that it is in breach of the fundamental right.

For a child-accused of an offence punishable with imprisonment of not more than 7 years, a period of 3 months from the date of filing of the complaint or lodging of the First Information Report is the maximum time permissible for investigation, and a period of 6 months from the filing of the charge sheet is a reasonable period within which the trial must be completed.
policy_considerations: The court recognized the special status of children, stating, 'If a child is a national asset, it is the duty of the State to look after the child with a view to ensuring full development of its personality.'

The court emphasized the severe harm caused by incarcerating children in jails: 'incarceration in jail would have the effect of dwarfing the development of the child, exposing him to baneful influences, coarsening his conscience and alienating him from the society.'

The court dismissed the State's potential excuses for delays, such as a lack of remand homes, stating, 'It is no answer on the part of the State to say that it has not got enough number of remand homes or observation homes or other places where children can be kept and that is why they are lodged in jails.'

The court acknowledged the systemic reasons for trial delays, such as 'the total inadequacy of judge-strength and lack of satisfactory working conditions,' 'heavy workload,' and courts working with 'depleted strength,' but did not accept these as valid reasons to deny the fundamental right to a speedy trial, particularly for children.
